newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Surgut issue seen holding back shares.
newsitem.headline: Surgut issue seen holding back shares.

text.p: Shares in Russian oil company OAO Surgutneftegaz fell further on Friday after Surgut Holding raised its stake in the company on Thursday and traders said the deal could have a negative impact on the entire market.

Surgut Holding (NK Surgutneftegaz) said on Thursday it had acquired an entire new issue of shares in Surgutneftegaz, Russia's second biggest oil company by sales, comprising 500 million ordinary shares and 34.02 million preferred shares.

The acquisition raised Surgut Holding's stake to 43.5 percent from 38 percent. A company official said there were no plans to place the shares in the secondary market. The price at which the shares were bought was not revealed.
"An effective if not actual dilution has taken place...To some extent, the trust of foreign investors will be undermined," said a Western analyst in Moscow.
Surgutneftegaz shares fell sharply on news of the issue on fears of increased supply, and concerns by existing shareholders that their stakes would be diluted.
Surgutneftegaz shares closed at $0.396 on Friday, down from $0.425 and breaking through what traders said was an important support level at $0.400. The shares closed on Wednesday at $0.462.
Surgutneftegaz preferred shares closed at $0.226 after Thursday's close at $0.232 and down from $0.290 on Wednesday.

"This is very bad for the whole market. One of the big worries of 1995 was the infringement of shareholders' right. Now one of the biggest companies has demonstrated disregard for its shareholders," said Pavel Gronbjerg, co-head equities trader at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

But traders said investor interest in the highly illiquid shares in Surgut Holding had increased. Instead of the one or two telephone calls a week, there had been six offers to buy the shares on Friday morning, one said.

Some analysts said the situation involving Surgut recalled a scandal in spring 1994 when oil company Komineft issued shares worth a nominal 10 billion roubles ($1.8 million). Some traders said at the time it diluted shareholdings by half.
Komineft insisted it had done nothing wrong.
Surgut, in common with other integrated Russian oil companies, is converting shares in its subsidiaries into those of the parent.
Traders said the new issue increased uncertainty.

"Of course, the price at which the shares was bought is important. But Surgut's basic problem is its unpredictability," said Dmitry Lobanov, chief trader in second-tier stocks at Alfa Kapital. ($ = 5454 Russian Roubles)
